name: Eriochloa

look_here_first: On Eriochloa species, look very closely at the short stem/pedicel just under a spikelet for a distinctive small cup- or ring-like collar. In TEXAS CUPGRASS (E. sericea), also look for a large non-rhizomatous bunch, soft folded/rolled leaves, a dense fringe of straight hairs for the true ligule, and fuzzy spikelets on narrow appressed racemes. Cup base requires high magnification: do not label it on distant whole-head photos.

recognition.where_to_look_first: Whole bunch → collar true ligule → narrow flowering head → one mature spikelet and its tiny basal cup/ring with 10–20× lens.
priority: perennial tuft from fibrous root mass, lacking creeping rhizomes
dense ring of straight hairs at ligule rather than a membrane
closely appressed slender racemes with soft/silky spikelets
small cup-like ring at each spikelet's base, requiring macro
zigzag remnant axis after spikelets drop (when seen)

comparison_lesson.memory_rule: BUNCH → HAIR LIGULE → FUZZY SEEDHEAD → TRUE SPIKELET CUP (macro).
quick_split: E. sericea — tufted perennial commonly about 0.3–1.2 m; soft blades, ring of straight ligular hairs, small fuzzy clustered spikelets on short hair-bearing stalks; tiny cup at spikelet base.
Paspalum spp. — can have spikelets in one-sided racemes but lack the diagnostic Eriochloa cup-like lower attachment; their ligule is generally membranous rather than a dense hair ring.
Digitaria spp. — often spreading grasses with fingerlike racemes and paired spikelets; no Eriochloa cup at each spikelet base. Inspect the same-plant base and spikelet attachments.
Panicum spp. — open or contracted panicles, but do not share the cup-like spikelet base; check spikelet, stalk, ligule with magnification.

what_to_teach_crew: The cup is NOT a cup-shaped flowering head. It is a tiny structure where the individual spikelet attaches near the pedicel; use 10–20× and a tiny ruler.
Texas cupgrass can look like another silky panicgrass without a true ligule and spikelet-base examination.
A dense hair ligule is a key vegetative cue, but don't mistake hairs around a node or blade base for the ligule itself.
Follow the specimen to its rooted bunch: no long creeping rhizomes for this Texas cupgrass concept.
After seed drop, the axis may appear zigzag; this alone is not species proof.
If a photo cannot resolve the cup, label only the flowering axis or individual spikelets.
